fixes.explanation: That's the reason, friend. Right after the blessing ask, the song says "that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." (Psalm 67:2). The blessing comes with a purpose attached, and the purpose looks way past "us." Think of it like a cookie box: it's made to be passed around, not hoarded in the pantry.

Rest sounds lovely, and I'd sign up for a nap myself. But the song doesn't say a word about rest or work. It asks God to bless "us," and gives the reason: "that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations." (Psalm 67:2). That reason reaches all the way out to the nations, friend.

Good guess, friend! Priests are a natural pick for a song about praise. But this chorus never mentions priests. It says, "Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You." (Psalm 67:3). The invitation is wide open, wider than any one group.

That's it, friend. The verse says "for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). So the nations get a Judge and a Leader. I'd follow that guide way before I'd follow my own sense of direction.

Scattering is a pretty scary picture, and the song doesn't paint it. It says "for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). Leading is the word, and it's part of why the song calls the nations to be glad and sing for joy.

Counting is a fair guess, but it's not in this verse. The song says "for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth." (Psalm 67:4). Leading the nations is what God does there, and that's the good news in the line.

You got it, friend. The last line says, "God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him." (Psalm 67:7). The song opens by asking God to bless "us," and it ends with the whole earth in view. That's a big finish.
